statement: A disjoncteur is a symmetric relation ⊥ on E such that x⊥x implies x⊥y for every y. For an irreflexive disjoncteur, the distinct nonorthogonal pairs give an arbitrary undirected simple graph. In general the data are such a graph plus a chosen subset E0 of its isolated vertices; loops of ⊥ occur exactly at E0. Thus graphs alone classify the irreflexive case, not all disjoncteurs. The unqualified final wording on line85 needs comparison with the qualifier on line81.

statement: A spatios is a complete lattice L with an order reversing involution C such that a∧Ca=0, equivalently a∨Ca=1. Then C exchanges arbitrary joins and meets and 0 with1. Defining a⊥b iff a≤Cb gives symmetric orthogonality, hereditary under decreasing either argument, with (∨iai)⊥b iff every ai⊥b; a⊥a forces a=0. Conversely these are the displayed disjoncteur properties for the underlying L.

his_statement: Corollaire1, conditions(i)–(v); E′ “dense” dans E.
statement: For D⊆E, the following precise conditions are equivalent: every closed S⊆E satisfies S=cE(S∩D); restriction ΣE→P(D) is injective; cE:ΣD→ΣE is surjective; and σE(D) is join-dense in ΣE. Then restriction and cE are inverse ortholattice isomorphisms. The lower-point condition says: for all x,y∈E, if every d∈D with d≼x is orthogonal to every e∈D with e≼y, then x⊥y. The manuscript’s (iv) “dense in the canonical preorder” is valid with joins evaluated in the ambient support lattice; interpreting it solely by intrinsic suprema in the point preorder need not be equivalent. The restriction to D in(v) is mathematically necessary but uncertain in the transcription.

statement: The missing pointwise equality fα(σE(x))=cFα(x) is exactly what permits passing from arbitrary-join preservation of fα to full closure commutation for α. Conversely, if f:ΣE→ΣF preserves all joins and α(x)=f(σE(x)), then fα=f and this equality holds. statement: For the OR product, closed rows and columns do not imply product closure in general. If either factor is trivial (x⊥y iff x≠y), they do imply product closure, since closure is computed rowwise or columnwise. Negative example: each factor has four points with only the paired orthogonalities0⊥1 and2⊥3; the three-point diagonal has closed fibers but empty perpendicular, hence full product closure.

This is an allowed finite orthomodular example, so even orthomodularity of the factors does not repair the universal statement.

statement: For a set E with trivial disjoncteur structure and a complete ortholattice M, evaluation on singleton subsets gives an order isomorphism Hom∨(P(E),M)≅M^E. Thus this Hom lattice is a complete ortholattice, with complement and orthogonality pointwise on the singleton values. The corresponding join map sends A to the join of those values indexed by A.

statement: For sets E,F, a union-preserving map u:P(E)→P(F) commutes with complements iff its singleton images form a pairwise disjoint partition of F. Equivalently u=v−1 for a unique function v:F→E. Dually the orthogonal transpose is a direct-image map. This is the algebraic characterization used to formulate the general span question.

his_statement: “Y-a-t-il une décomposition similaire ... entre spatios ?”
statement: With comorphisms defined as arbitrary-join maps commuting with C and morphisms their orthogonal transposes, ask whether every join map f:L→M factors as h†∘g through some complete ortholattice K, where g:L→K and h:M→K commute with C. The answer is no. Let L=M be the six-element four-atom ortholattice with atoms a,b,c,d, and f(0)=f(a)=0, f(b)=f(c)=f(d)=f(1)=a. This preserves all joins. Any nontrivial K and C-preserving join map h:L→K has zero kernel, hence h†(1)=1; since g(1)=1, such a factorization would give f(1)=1. Trivial K gives the zero composite. Thus no K works.
